For more information, see [Use the System File Checker tool to repair missing or corrupted system files](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/use-the-system-file-checker-tool-to-repair-missing-or-corrupted-system-files-79aa86cb-ca52-166a-92a3-966e85d4094e) on the Microsoft website.\\n* Individual KB updates fail and return \\\"-2145124475\\\" or \\\"0x800f0985\\\" error messages.\\n\\nTo check for corrupted system files, complete the following steps:\\n\\n1. Review your CBS logs at %systemroot%\\\\\\\\Logs\\\\\\\\CBS.\\n2. In your logs, look for **CSI Payload Corrupt** entries.\\n3. Run the System File Checker command to identify and repair corrupt system files: \\n ```plaintext\\n sfc /scannow\\n ```\\n **Note:** If the System File Checker command doesn't repair the corrupt system files that it finds, then rerun the command. If the command can't repair your system files after three tries, then proceed to the next step.\\n4. Run the following **CheckHealth** command to check the Component Store of the Windows image for corrupt files: \\n ```plaintext\\n DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /CheckHealth\\n ```\\n **Note:** For information, see [/Cleanup-Image](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/dism-operating-system-package-servicing-command-line-options?view=windows-11#cleanup-image) on the Microsoft website.\\n5. If the **CheckHealth** command detects corruption, then run the following **ScanHealth** command to check that the image is repairable: \\n `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /ScanHealth` \\n If the image is repairable, run the following **RestoreHealth** command: \\n `DISM /Online /Cleanup\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/systems-manager-patch-install-fail\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Migrating Windows Server 2008 to AWS: Resolving PV Driver Issues and Boot Failures | Migration & Modernization\",\"context\":\"### Issue 3: Corrupt SYSTEM Registry Hive (Error 0xc000014c)\\n\\n**Symptom:** \u201cWindows failed to load because the system registry file is missing, or corrupt.\u201d\\n\\n**Root cause:** The SYSTEM registry hive was corrupted during the MGN conversion process.\\n\\n**Fix:** Restore from the Windows registry backup:\\n\\n`copy E:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\config\\\\RegBack\\\\system E:\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\config\\\\system /Y`\\n\\nIf you previously modified driver startup types (Issue 2), the RegBack copy will overwrite those changes. {"id": "0d1749a0-f0a0-408a-a495-da72b4bd76af", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Looping `RestoreHealth` without progress almost always means DISM can't find good source files on Windows Update to pull from — repeating it just re-runs the same failed download. Here's the right escalation path:

**1. Confirm it's actually a component store issue, not something else**
Check `%systemroot%\Logs\CBS\CBS.log` for `CSI Payload Corrupt` entries — if `ScanHealth` is reporting corruption, you'll see these there with the specific corrupt component GUIDs/payloads.

**2. Give RestoreHealth a real source instead of relying on Windows Update**
If your instance has no internet path to Windows Update (or WU itself is the thing that's broken), `RestoreHealth` has nothing to repair from and will just loop. Point it at a known-good source:
```
DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth /Source:WIM:D:\sources\install.wim:1 /LimitAccess
```
using the install media for the exact same build/edition of Server 2016 (match the build number — this matters a lot for 2016 since there are several cumulative-update baselines). `/LimitAccess` stops it from reaching out to Windows Update and forces it to use only your source.

**3. If DISM still can't repair it, run SFC against that same source**
```
sfc /scannow
```
run it up to 3 times. SFC and DISM complement each other — SFC can fix files DISM's component store repair doesn't touch, and vice versa.

**4. If it's still looping after a valid offline source + SFC**
At that point the component store itself is likely too damaged to self-heal online, and continuing to retry `RestoreHealth` won't converge. The reliable path is an **offline repair via EC2Rescue for Windows Server**:
- Stop the instance, detach the EBS root volume, attach it to a healthy helper instance running EC2Rescue
- Run EC2Rescue's **Offline Instance** repair against that volume
- Reattach the volume to the original instance

This avoids trying to repair a live, half-corrupted servicing stack from inside itself, which is usually why the loop never resolves.

A couple of things worth checking before you go the EC2Rescue route — do you want me to look at whether this instance has outbound access to Windows Update endpoints, or pull the actual CBS.log corruption entries if you can get me a snippet?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
